voyage.title: Jacques Cartier and the St Lawrence (1534-1542)
voyage.ships: La Grande Hermine and the ships of three voyages from Saint-Malo
voyage.sponsor: sailing from Saint-Malo for King Francis I of France
voyage.summary: Three voyages into the Gulf of St Lawrence and up the river: the cross raised at Gaspé, the winter at Stadacona and the scurvy that was cured by an Iroquoian remedy, the journey to Hochelaga beneath the mountain Cartier named Mont Royal, and the failed colony of Charlesbourg-Royal.
voyage.what_was_lost: Cartier wrote the relations of the first two voyages himself; the third survives only through Hakluyt's English translation of an original now lost. The St Lawrence Iroquoians who met him left no account — not Donnacona, whom Cartier carried to France where he died, nor the people of Stadacona and Hochelaga, who had vanished from the valley before Champlain arrived sixty years later, for reasons no surviving document explains.

waypoints.event: Jacques Cartier and his crew returned to the harbour of St. Malo, completing their first voyage of exploration to the land they called New France.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: that we reached the harbour of St. Malo whence we had set forth, on [Saturday] September 5 in the said year [1534].
waypoints.diary_source_citation: The Voyages of Jacques Cartier (ed. H. P. Biggar, Public Archives of Canada, 1924)

waypoints.place_modern: Cape Bonavista, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada
waypoints.event: Jacques Cartier arrived at Cape Bonavista, Newfoundland, marking one of his first landfalls in the New World during his 1534 voyage.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: It is still called cape Bonavista and lies in latitude 48° 42’ 27”. The name is given on the Viegas, Riccardiana, Desliens, Vallard and Mercator maps and on the Desceliers planisphere.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: The Voyages of Jacques Cartier (ed. H. P. Biggar, Public Archives of Canada, 1924)

waypoints.place_modern: Îles aux Oiseaux (Bird Rocks), Quebec, Canada
Strait of Belle Isle, Newfoundland and Labrador/Quebec, Canada
waypoints.event: Jacques Cartier's expedition entered the Strait of Belle Isle, marking their passage from the Atlantic into the Gulf of St. Lawrence and making known the existence of open water over a vast area.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: The strait of Belle Isle with that portion of the gulf of St. Lawrence lying just inside the strait. The name was a most natural one if it be borne in mind that those who first made their way from the Atlantic through this strait into the gulf were quite unaware both of the extension of that inland water as far as Cabot strait and of the existence of the river St. Lawrence. This west end of the strait naturally appeared to them therefore to form a “ Big Bay.”
waypoints.diary_source_citation: The Voyages of Jacques Cartier (ed. H. P. Biggar, Public Archives of Canada, 1924)

waypoints.event: Cartier and his crew sighted and named the island 'Assumption island' (now Anticosti Island) during their exploration of the Gulf of St. Lawrence.

waypoints.place_modern: Belle Isle, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada
waypoints.event: The expedition reached Belle-Isle at the entrance to the Strait of Belle Isle, a key landmark between Newfoundland and the coast of Labrador, which was noted as an important point for navigation and fishing.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: one Island in the very entrie of the streight called Belle Isle, which places if they be peopled and well fortified . . . wee shall be lordes of the whole fishing in small time,” in Hakluyt, op. cit., III, 134.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: The Voyages of Jacques Cartier (ed. H. P. Biggar, Public Archives of Canada, 1924)

waypoints.event: Jacques Cartier and his crew completed their voyage and returned to the harbour of St. Malo, from where they had originally set out.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: that we reached the harbour of St. Malo whence we had set forth, on [Saturday] September 5 in the said year [1534].
waypoints.diary_source_citation: The Voyages of Jacques Cartier (ed. H. P. Biggar, Public Archives of Canada, 1924)

waypoints.event: Cartier and his crew completed their return voyage and arrived back at the harbour of St. Malo, France, from which they had originally set forth.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: and entered a harbour called Rougnouse +”, where we took on board . wood and fresh water for consumption at sea. Here we left one of our long-boats'®. And on Monday, the nineteenth of that month [of June], we set forth from this [Renewse] harbour and were favoured at sea with such good weather that we reached St. Malo on [Sunday] July 161°, 1536, thanks be to God, whom we implore on bringing our voyage to an end, to give us His grace and His paradise hereafter. Amen.

waypoints.place_modern: Funk Island, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada
waypoints.event: Cartier's expedition arrived at the Isle of Birds (Funk Island), where they found an incredible number of seabirds and collected many for food, salting several casks full.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: And on [Thursday] the twenty-first of the said month of May we set forth from this [Catalina] harbour with a west wind, and sailed north, one quarter north-east of cape Bonavista as far as the isle of Birds!, which island was completely surrounded and encompassed by a cordon of loose ice, split up into cakes. waypoints.diary_source_citation: The Voyages of Jacques Cartier (ed. H. P. Biggar, Public Archives of Canada, 1924)

waypoints.event: The expedition explored and described Anticosti Island, noting its geography and the presence of a large bay with good anchorage. The island was recognized as significant for navigation in the Gulf of St. Lawrence.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: Anticosti island which is 135 miles long and about thirty miles in width at the broadest part.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: The Voyages of Jacques Cartier (ed. H. P. Biggar, Public Archives of Canada, 1924)

waypoints.event: Cartier and his party learned from local chiefs about the Saguenay River, its navigability, and its connection to the legendary kingdom of Saguenay, while traveling and interacting with tribes near their ships after returning from Hochelaga.

waypoints.diary_source_citation: The Voyages of Jacques Cartier (ed. H. P. Biggar, Public Archives of Canada, 1924)

waypoints.event: Cartier and his crew arrived and anchored at the foot of the island of Orleans, a key waypoint as they ascended the St. Lawrence River toward Stadacona.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: On Saturday, May 6, we set sail from Stef Croix harbour ®®, and came to anchor at the foot of the island of Orleans®’, some twelve leagues from Ste. Croix.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: The Voyages of Jacques Cartier (ed. H. P. Biggar, Public Archives of Canada, 1924)

waypoints.event: Jacques Cartier and his men visited the village of Stadacona, home of Donnacona and his people, which stood about half a league from where their ships were anchored near the St. Charles River.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: he Captain, accompanied by the gentlemen and with fifty sailors drawn up in order, went to visit Donnacona and his people at their home called Stada- cona!®, which stood about half a league from the spot where lay our ships. And on drawing near the village, the inhabitants

And on Monday, the nineteenth of that month [of June], we set forth from this [Renewse] harbour and were favoured at sea with such good weather that we reached St. Malo on [Sunday] July 161°, 1536, thanks be to God, whom we implore on bringing our voyage to an end, to give us His grace and His paradise hereafter. waypoints.event: Cartier and his fleet departed from St. Malo, Brittany, France, at the start of his third voyage to Canada in May 1541, after being given full authority by Monsieur Roberval.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: After these things thus dispatched, the winde comming faire, the foresayd five ships set sayle together well furnished and victualled for two yeare, the 23. of May, 15407. And we sailed so long with contrary winds and continuall torments, which fell out by reason of our late departure, that wee were on the sea with our sayd five ships full three moneths before wee could arriv
waypoints.diary_source_citation: The Voyages of Jacques Cartier (ed. H. P. Biggar, Public Archives of Canada, 1924)

waypoints.event: Cartier and his expedition arrived at the village of Stadacona, located beneath the north brow of Cape Diamond, where they interacted with the local inhabitants and remained for an extended period.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: This village is called Stada- cona’?. And before reaching this point, there are four tribes and villages, namely: Ajoaste, Starnatam, Tailla, which is on a moun- tain, and Sitadin. Then the village of Stadacona. Beneath this high land on the north lies the river and harbour of Ste. Croix [St. Charles], where we remained with our ships hauled out, as before mentioned, from September 15, [1535] until May 6, 1536.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: The Voyages of Jacques Cartier (ed. H. P. Biggar, Public Archives of Canada, 1924)

waypoints.place_historical: the building on the river of Cape Rouge and in the one on the cliff above
waypoints.event: Cartier's men began building a fort at the mouth of the Cape Rouge river, establishing Charlesbourg-Royal, and suffered from scurvy and harsh conditions during the winter.
waypoints.diary_excerpt: That is in the mess below in the building on the river of Cape Rouge and in the one on the cliff above.
waypoints.diary_source_citation: The Voyages of Jacques Cartier (ed. H. P. Biggar, Public Archives of Canada, 1924)
